audit.reasoning: Coding 'fixed-strict' initial primary stress rests on the right work — Tyler 1969, the standard (and only) reference grammar of Koya, dedicated stress section pp. 32-33 — and is corroborated by the Hayes 1980 text we hold ('Primary stress falls on the initial syllable, secondary stress on closed syllables or syllables with a long vowel'), which StressTyp2 quotes verbatim (confirmed in held scanned). Nothing found contradicts it: the three other held Koya descriptions (Rama Rao 1979, Baskaran 2002, Subrahmanyam 1968) say nothing about stress, and no later phonology/instrumental study of Koya prosody surfaced. sources.quote: p. 32: "Stress. There are two types of stress - strong and weak. Stress is predictable on the basis of juncture, syllable quantity, and pitch. Consequently, it is not phonemic. In a phrase strong stress regularly occurs on the first syllable, each fol-lowing syllable being more lightly stressed, but still distinguishable from weak stress. Within a word stress occurs with long syllables, i.e., (C)V, CVC, CVC, CVNC. Syllabic prominence occurs on vowels. Weak stress occurs with short syllables." p.
sources.note: This IS the deciding source, but our quotation is a Google Books snippet reconstruction (macrons lost in the syllable templates '(C)V, CVC, CVC, CVNC') and no page scan is banked; a scan of pp. 32-33 would make the quote verifiable and settle the domain field (Tyler frames strong stress as phrase-initial: 'In a phrase strong stress regularly occurs on the first syllable'), currently not stated by the source in the record.
